Text: With age, taste buds become less sensitive to {{c1::salty}} and {{c1::sweet}} foods, and food may be perceived as bland and flavorless because the sense of {{c2::smell}} fades along with taste.
Back Extra:
Why: dulled flavor is one of the age-related changes in gastric and intestinal function that together inhibit nutritional intake and utilization.

Ex: tooth loss makes chewing harder, decreased saliva impairs the breakdown of complex carbohydrates, and gastric acid secretion diminishes.

Text: {{c1::Peristalsis}} is the process in which intestinal contractions {{c2::move food along the digestive tract}}, and with age it {{c3::slows::speeds up or slows}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the aging gut changes in more ways than its speed — gallstones become increasingly common, and a less elastic anal sphincter can lead to fecal incontinence.

Text: Age-related change in peristalsis leaves an older adult prone to {{c1::constipation::bowel}} and/or {{c1::suppressed feelings of hunger::appetite}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: constipation and a poor appetite in an older adult are easy to write off as habit or mood, when one normal age change in the gut produces both.

Distinguish: appetite loss from peristalsis is a gut-motility effect, separate from the fading smell and taste that makes food seem bland.

Text: In older adults, blood flow to the intestines can drop by as much as {{c1::50%}}, so the extraction of {{c2::vitamins}} and {{c2::minerals}} from digested food wanes.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the 50% belongs to intestinal blood flow, not to the renal figures for kidney size and filtration — keep each number tied to its organ.

Why: absorption depends on perfusion, so an older adult can take in enough food and still absorb fewer vitamins and minerals from it.

Text: Between the ages of 20 and 90 years, the kidneys decrease in size by {{c1::20%}} and their filtration capabilities decline by as much as {{c1::50%}}.
Back Extra:
Why: blood supply to the nephrons falls, and the number of nephrons itself declines between the ages of 30 and 80 years.

Pitfall: do not swap the two numbers. The 20% is anatomic (a smaller kidney) and the up-to-50% is functional (less filtering).

Text: Aging reduces renal function in two ways: the kidneys become less able to {{c1::remove waste}} from the body and less able to {{c1::conserve fluids}} when needed.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the kidney filters blood inside its nephrons, and aging both shrinks their blood supply and reduces their number.

Pitfall: the fluid-conservation half is the one that gets forgotten, so an older adult who is losing volume also struggles to hold on to what is left.

Text: By the time a person is {{c1::80}} years of age, the brain has decreased in weight by as much as {{c2::10% to 20%}}.
Back Extra:
Why: motor and sensory neural networks become slower and less responsive over the same span of years.

Distinguish: an infant brain holds more neurons than an adult brain, yet the adult brain is far more flexible, because the number of interconnections between neurons increases with age.

Text: In an older adult, the brain's metabolic rate and oxygen consumption remain {{c1::unchanged::increased, decreased, or unchanged}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: aging changes the speed of the brain's neural networks, not its metabolic demand — motor and sensory networks become slower and less responsive while oxygen use holds steady.

Pitfall: a lighter, slower older brain is not a less oxygen-hungry one.

Text: In an older adult, age-related {{c1::shrinkage}} of the brain opens a void between the brain and the outermost layer of the meninges, so a rapid or forceful shift of the brain can tear the {{c2::bridging veins}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: at every other age the cranial vault is almost entirely occupied by the brain, the meningeal layers, and the cerebrospinal fluid between them, so there is virtually no empty space.

Mechanism: the void gives the brain room to move inside the cranium, which is the step that turns a rapid or forceful shift into a torn vein.

Text: An 82-year-old struck her head on a cabinet door and is alert with no complaints. In an older adult, bleeding around the brain after a head impact {{c1::may go unnoticed for some time::how it presents}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a normal exam soon after a head impact does not clear an older patient, because blood can accumulate quietly in the space that opens around an aging brain.

Mechanism: the bleeding runs into that open space instead of pressing against a tightly packed cranial vault, which is why the signs arrive late.
